title: Australia’s Greater Gliders Fly Majestically From Tree to Tree—And Now We Know Exactly How Far
gist: A study in Australian Mammalogy measured 41 southern greater glider leaps, finding average launch height of 71.5 feet, landing at 15.4 feet, average glide distance 62.7 feet and a maximum horizontal distance of 162.7 feet — shorter than previously assumed, per the article's standfirst. The piece is a brief write-up truncated at Nautilus's paywall.

insights.claim: Researchers recorded 41 tree-to-tree leaps by southern greater gliders, launching from an average height of 71.5 feet, landing at an average of 15.4 feet, and covering an average distance of 62.7 feet.
insights.speaker: David Nield
insights.so_what: First hard numbers for the species' movement envelope — the input any habitat-connectivity or canopy-gap standard would have to use.
insights.locator: In a new study published in Australian Mammalogy

insights.claim: The maximum horizontal distance covered in a single recorded greater glider glide was 162.7 feet, roughly 2.6 times the measured average.
insights.speaker: David Nield
insights.so_what: The gap between average and maximum matters for corridor design — planning to the mean would strand animals most of the time.
insights.locator: the maximum horizontal distance covered in a glide was 162.7 feet

insights.claim: The measured glide distances are shorter than previously assumed for the species, so the new data revises expectations downward rather than confirming them.
insights.speaker: David Nield
insights.so_what: Downward revision means existing forest-corridor gaps may be wider than the animals can actually cross — a tightening constraint on logging and land-clearing approvals.
insights.quote: It’s not as far as we thought, though
insights.locator: It’s not as far as we thought, though (standfirst)

insights.claim: The southern greater glider (Petauroides volans) is a nocturnal marsupial native to southeastern Australian forests that glides using a flexible membrane fixed between its forearms and hind legs.
insights.speaker: David Nield
insights.so_what: An obligate canopy-glider confined to southeastern Australian forest is directly exposed to native-forest harvesting policy in Victoria and New South Wales.
insights.locator: The southern greater glider (Petauroides volans) is a nocturnal marsupial
